extracted.intended_audience: academic mathematicians who write letters of recommendation and/or serve as journal/book editors and referees
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writing effective academic letters of recommendation (for faculty, students, tenure/job cases) and for performing editorial duties (managing editors, associate editors, referees, and proceedings/book editors) in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of possible candidate access to letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Inform the letter-writer up front if, in some states/institutions, the candidate may have access to the complete text of the letter and the identities of writers; give the writer the option to decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the soliciting school permits candidate access to letters, the school will inform the writer when requesting the letter. The writer may decline to write if uncomfortable with this situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague praise ('damning with faint praise')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write vague, generic praise that says nothing substantive; such letters can be construed as negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague phrases (e.g., 'he's a hail-fellow, well met') undercut the writer's responsibility and force evaluators to guess intent. Detailed, specific remarks make misconstrual difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity about research and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Make concrete comments about specific work or papers, particular qualities, specific contributions, and objective academic qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dwell (perhaps a page or more) on virtues of the candidate's scientific work: why a result is important, how it improves earlier work, how it advances the field, who else has worked on the problem. Because many readers are nonspecialists, briefly give background and motivation and mention reputable publication venues when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use binary comparisons / rank among peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the candidate to other named individuals of similar age/career level (preferably recognized academic peers), and if appropriate place them in a ranked group (e.g., 'one of the five best under 35').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete comparisons (e.g., 'comparable to David Mumford at the same age') provide immediate understanding and impact. Avoid obscure or culturally specific comparisons. If you must, state relative position (e.g., 'number 15') rather than remaining silent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor letter to the soliciting institution's expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the soliciting letter and address the topics the institution cares about (research vs teaching emphasis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the request is from a teaching college, focus on teaching, curriculum, appropriate (teaching-oriented) publications, and other items they value; avoid lengthy technical discussions irrelevant to their mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide credible evidence of teaching ability
rubrics_metrics.description: When relevant, supply concrete evidence about the candidate's teaching: awards, colleague testimony, or other specific information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are not in the candidate's department, derive credible evidence from colleagues' reports or documented awards. Detailed, knowledgeable comments about teaching make a strong impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be candid: negative letters have strong effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Be honest and decisive in negative evaluations: a single negative letter can often stop a tenure/hiring case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not soften a negative view by assuming it will matter only if others agree. One clear negative assessment can be decisive; therefore, call it as you see it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a recognizable, truthful letter-writing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate an individual style but always be truthful and avoid repeatedly sending the same boilerplate letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The community mentally tracks letter-writers' reputations. If your letters are always identical or uniformly flattering, they will be ignored. Being known to 'tell it like it is' increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student letters must be specifically informative (no binary comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing letters for students (undergraduates/graduate students), give specific, memorable, and credible details since binary comparisons are often inappropriate or ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples of achievement (e.g., novel proofs discovered, problems posed, exceptional performance outside standard coursework). Saying a student is one of the best you've taught is useful; transcript grades alone are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor letters for job-seeking students: key content
rubrics_metrics.description: Thesis-advisor letters should explain why the student is strong, what they have accomplished, and, if credible, compare them favorably to recent degree-holders; also address teaching and collegial interaction abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure outside letter-writers know what's in the thesis; where possible, secure letters from other institutions; include detailed letters about teaching ability to strengthen the dossier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest assessment of language/communication skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurately report a candidate's ability to speak and communicate in English (or relevant language), particularly where teaching or TA duties are concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overgeneralized praise ('excellent English') if untrue. Present facts gently but clearly about the candidate’s comprehension and classroom communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor responsibilities across the publication process
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors add value at each stage: choosing reviewers, evaluating reports, overseeing rewriting, deciding series/issue placement, maintaining paper flow and quality, adjudicating priority disputes, and overseeing production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors act as intermediaries between authors and publishers, shepherd manuscripts through review and production, and are accountable to the publishing organization for quality and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing editor duties and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Managing Editor oversees the journal's entire academic operation, supervises associate editors, makes final publication decisions, and handles issues like plagiarism, fraud, and priority disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managing Editors must monitor paper flow and acceptance rates (which affect reputation), ensure enough papers for timely issues, and intervene where AEs or refereeing processes stall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate editor responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate Editors are assigned papers to handle: they find referees, solicit reports, evaluate those reports, and recommend accept/reject to the Managing Editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A typical AE handles ~10–20 papers/year, generally should not act as the referee except occasionally, and must be able to find suitable referees and manage the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Select referees who are subject-matter experts, dependable, impartial, and capable of completing the review in a timely fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If names are not obvious, use the paper’s references, MathSciNet searches, or colleagues to identify potential referees. Avoid referees with conflicts or prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee management and tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep careful track of referees' assignments and timings to manage paper flow efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spreadsheets, electronic editorial systems, calendars, or project-management tools (e.g., Gantt charts) to monitor who has a paper and for how long; intervene when delays occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee reports must be substantive: put the paper in context, state whether results are significant, identify specific merits or faults, and reach a clear recommendation (accept/reject) with reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length should suit the paper (e.g., a short paper may need only one page of report). Avoid perfunctory reports ('I read some of this paper...') which are unhelpful. See referenced Section 4.10 for key points to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' use and editing of referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must be able to interpret, summarize, edit, or paraphrase referee reports—protecting anonymity and toning unnecessarily harsh language—so authors receive useful, professional feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reports are incisive and detailed, AE may act on them; if not, an AE might read the paper or seek another referee. Editing reports to remove identity-compromising or insulting remarks is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive rejection correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a paper, provide a courteous, constructive letter that encloses the referee report(s), cites specific weaknesses or errata, and suggests possible improvements or alternative venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to help the author preserve dignity and learn from the experience; be specific about problems (e.g., serious gaps) and offer actionable guidance where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit instructions to referees; rely on their judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overburdening referees with rigid instructions about report form; request that they assess significance and context and let them provide the substantive advice the editor can use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not micromanage referees; instead, take the submitted reports and make editorial use of them (including editing/paraphrasing when necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference proceedings editing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: For proceedings, demand refereeing, set and enforce page limits, encourage some participants to write survey articles, and provide a strong, informative introduction to the volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reciprocal/referee assignments among participants to obtain constructive reviews while maintaining fairness; enforce page limits to avoid overly long contributions; make the introduction 3–4+ pages and focus the volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript preparation checklist (AMS items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a preparation checklist addressing technical and administrative details: page/type block size, careful proofreading, permissions, figure rendering and resolution, acknowledgment of grant/contract support, and inclusion of MSC numbers and keywords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AMS checklist is a useful touchstone for proceedings or book preparation. Also ensure figures are in proper format (PostScript) and resolution, obtain required permissions, and include classification numbers and keywords.
